findings:

materiality:

risks:

dissent:

required\_changes:

verification:

acceptance\_criteria:

stop\_condition:

recommended\_next\_state:



17\. Legacy-to-Modern Transition Rules



The v1.12.00 PBIM contains useful historical mechanisms but also contains inconsistencies and legacy assumptions. The following transition is mandatory.



Legacy practice



Modern PBIM treatment



Fixed “40 processes” claim



Retain historical mapping as compatibility data; do not represent it as the current PMBOK 8 architecture.



Later reference to “49 processes”



Treat as a legacy/internal classification candidate until the project registry establishes the authoritative mapping.



Process ID used as document identity



Separate project/task/document/lifecycle/process classification.



main/<agent-name> as universal workflow



Treat branches as implementation details; authority comes from governance and task controls.



Agent approval as ultimate authority



Replace with human accountability plus independent assurance.



90% AEC pass threshold



Replace with materiality-based gates; blockers cannot be averaged away.



Empty mandatory sections



Prohibited in operating templates; explicitly classify deferred/non-applicable items.



Symbolic branch/tag as durable reference



Add immutable commit SHA/tag object identifier.



Policy-only Task Packet



Add enforceable scope checks and CI evidence.



Abstract H0 role



Instantiate Human Authority Register before charter readiness.



Emergency delegate without strict expiry



Apply bounded delegation and 72-hour default hard limit.



“Implementation verified” as release readiness



Separate design verification, implementation verification, operational readiness, and release authorization.



Generic global compliance



Apply \[PROJECT-LOCATION] law/regulation first.



AI as implementation authority



AI is bounded execution/analysis capability under human governance.



The adversarial results specifically identified durable-reference integrity, CI task-scope enforcement, operational readiness, light-governance reinstatement, emergency delegation, and human authority population as material closure concerns. These controls are therefore incorporated into this baseline rather than left as optional notes.



18\. Change Control for PBIM Itself



A PBIM baseline change is classified as:



MINOR — editorial/non-semantic.



CONTROL — modifies a control without changing authority architecture.



MATERIAL — changes a load-bearing process, identifier, authority, security, evidence, or lifecycle rule.



CONSTITUTIONAL — changes fundamental governance authority or protected PBIM rules.



Material and constitutional changes require AEA/AEV/AEC/AECC treatment proportionate to their impact.



A load-bearing assumption failure triggers ARCHITECTURAL RESET.

Before release of any PBIM version, confirm:



Structure



Every mandatory section has an identifier.



Identifiers are unique.



Identifier semantics are documented.



Sequence is machine-readable.



No contradictory process-count claim exists.



PBIM ends at 0004.1.



Engineering



Architecture is internally coherent.



Requirements are traceable.



Security boundary is explicit.



Privacy obligations are explicit.



AI governance is explicit where relevant.



Operational readiness is explicit.



Recovery/reset is explicit.



Governance



H0 is instantiated.



Authority is separated from capability.



Agent roles are bounded.



Dissent is preserved.



Stop controls are defined.



Emergency authority is bounded.



Evidence



Sources are traceable.



Durable references are immutable or hash-pinned.



Evidence classification is present.



Material decisions have acceptance criteria.



Superseded artifacts remain discoverable.



Local compliance



\[PROJECT-LOCATION] identified.



Applicable laws identified.



Regulatory authorities identified.



Sector-specific obligations assessed.



Privacy/data requirements assessed.



Cybersecurity requirements assessed.



Electronic transaction requirements assessed where relevant.

Primary responsibility



Lead Agent



architecture, synthesis, orchestration, decision preparation



Security/Challenge Agent



adversarial challenge, security attack, threat analysis



Reliability/Verification Agent



independent verification, testing, CI/reliability



Implementation Agent



bounded implementation within Task Packet



Human H0



accountable project authority



Human H1/HA



delegated/review/specialist authority



The roster is configurable.



Agent names are not constitutional. A project may replace tools without changing governance semantics.



24\. Independence Requirements



Independence shall be evaluated explicitly.



At minimum assess:



organizational independence;



credential/access independence;



decision-right independence;



evidence independence.



A reviewer who cannot independently access the evidence necessary to challenge a baseline is not fully independent.



Multiple agents repeating the same incorrect assumption do not constitute independent confirmation.



25\. Operational Readiness Model



The project shall distinguish:



DESIGN-VERIFIED

&#x20;       ↓

IMPLEMENTATION-VERIFIED

&#x20;       ↓

OPERATIONALLY-READY

&#x20;       ↓

RELEASE-AUTHORIZED

&#x20;       ↓

PRODUCTION



No state may be inferred from the previous state.



For high-assurance work, operational readiness should include:



monitoring;



alerting;



rollback;



recovery;



backup;



incident response;



access control;



support ownership;



documentation;



dependency availability;



data-protection checks;



security acceptance;



human release authorization.



26\. Decision Ledger



Material decisions shall record:



decision\_id:

date:

project\_id:

decision:

decision\_type:

authority:

contributors:

evidence:

alternatives:

risk:

conditions:

effective\_state:

supersedes:

review\_date:

integrity\_hash:



The ledger must preserve both the decision and material dissent.



27\. Architectural Reset



An Architectural Reset is not a failure of the project-management system. It is a controlled recovery mechanism.



Trigger conditions include:



load-bearing assumption invalidated;



critical security defect;



legal incompatibility;



authority ambiguity;



corrupted identifier registry;



material evidence-integrity failure;



AEC discovers an architecture-breaking condition;



production behavior disproves a foundational architectural assumption.



Reset sequence:



STOP

↓

PRESERVE EVIDENCE

↓

INVALIDATE AFFECTED BASELINE

↓

RECORD FAILED ASSUMPTION

↓

AEA

↓

AEV

↓

AEC

↓

AECC

↓

RESUME / RETURN / TERMINATE



28\. PBIM Completion Criteria



PBIM is complete only when:



the generic baseline is internally coherent;



the project-specific proposal exists;



the project-specific template exists;



authority is instantiated;



compliance applicability is established;



security/data boundaries are defined;



identifiers are registered;



governance controls are operationally instantiated to the required maturity;



simulation/readiness review is complete;



material blockers are closed;



charter inputs are ready;



H0 authorizes transition.

(DEVELOP PROJECT CHARTER)

Canonical PBIM Identifier Grammar



The v1.12 identifier model is retained conceptually but normalized so that one identifier grammar and one registry are authoritative.

0.4 Lifecycle Semantics



PBIM uses two complementary structures:



A. Operational lifecycle: the actual sequence through which PBIM work is performed.



B. PM/standards mapping: a traceability map showing how PBIM activities align with recognized project-management practices.



The PM-process mapping is not the primary workflow engine. This resolves the v1.12 problem in which process-number sequencing was allowed to become the lifecycle itself.



0.5 Control Maturity



PBIM uses four maturity states:



DESIGNED — the control is defined.



ENFORCEABLE — the control has an executable mechanism, schema, gate, permission rule, workflow, or task packet.



ENFORCED — the control is active in the authoritative project environment and can block unauthorized progression.



INDEPENDENTLY-VERIFIED — an appropriately independent assurance function has verified that the control operates as claimed.



No document may claim ENFORCED or INDEPENDENTLY-VERIFIED solely because the control is described.



0.6 Evidence Rule



For every material governance decision, retain the original evidence where technically and legally permissible.



Material evidence SHOULD record:



source artifact;



source location;



content/integrity hash where appropriate;



original timestamp;



author or originating system;



verifier;



verification result;



applicable revision;



retention classification;



access classification;



supersession relationship.



A summary is not a substitute for retained source evidence.



1\. GOVERNANCE CONSTITUTION



1.1 Governance → Assurance → Execution



PBIM separates three functions:



Governance establishes authority, constraints, priorities, approvals, and stop conditions.



Assurance independently examines governance, architecture, requirements, evidence, security, risk, compliance, and implementation readiness.



Execution performs authorized project work.



Technical capability does not create governance authority.



Agent consensus does not create governance authority.



A role title does not automatically create independence.



1.2 Constitutional Authority \[CA]



PBIM MUST have a Constitutional Authority outside ordinary PBIM project execution.



CA → PBIM → Project Authority / Assurance / Execution



The CA is the constitutional root for PBIM itself. PBIM MUST NOT invent a higher authority merely to resolve a compromise of CA.



Before a project reaches CHARTER-READY, the Governance Repository MUST contain:



CA identity;



appointing organization;



accountable principal;



authority source;



authority scope;



appointment evidence;



effective date;



review/expiry date;



succession or availability procedure;



conflict declaration, where applicable.



If a valid CA record does not exist:



CONSTITUTIONAL-AUTHORITY-BLOCKED



Constitutional changes MUST stop.



1.3 CA Unavailability



CA unavailability MUST NOT automatically transfer CA powers to a project manager, lead agent, repository administrator, or emergency operator.



Unless a pre-authorized succession mechanism exists:



CA UNAVAILABLE → CONSTITUTIONAL-BLOCKED



If succession exists, it MUST be:



pre-authorized;



time-bounded;



scope-bounded;



recorded;



independently verifiable.



1.4 Human Project Authority \[H0]



H0 is the principal human project authority within the authorized project scope.



H0 may:



authorize project-level governance actions;



approve defined project decisions;



resolve project-level escalations;



authorize bounded emergency procedures;



sponsor the charter process.



H0 MUST NOT:



redefine CA;



remove CA;



bypass protected constitutional controls;



convert technical access into governance authority;



approve evidence that the authority matrix says requires independent approval.



1.5 Authority vs Technical Capability



PBIM MUST maintain a distinction between:



Governance authority



and



Technical capability.



Technical capabilities can include:



repository administration;



organization administration;



infrastructure administration;



CI/CD administration;



database administration;



deployment access;



cloud administration;



automation credentials.



Possession of such capability does not itself confer approval authority.



2\. AUTHORITATIVE REGISTERS AND PROTECTED CONTROLS



2.1 Governance Repository



The project MUST identify one authoritative Governance Repository or an explicitly defined set of repositories governed by one canonical precedence rule.



It MUST contain or reference:



PBIM baseline;



identifier registry;



authority register;



authority-permission matrix;



decision ledger;



authoritative ADRs;



requirements/constraints register;



risk register;



stakeholder register;



regulatory/compliance register;



evidence index;



task-packet state;



gate records;



AEA/AEV/AEC/AECC artifacts;



project proposal;



project template;



project charter package.



2.2 Authority Register



The Authority Register records:



principal;



organizational role;



governance authority;



delegated authority;



technical identity;



scope;



environment;



approval rights;



expiration/review date;



conflicts;



evidence of appointment.



2.3 Authority–Permission Matrix



The matrix maps:



Principal → Authority → Technical Identity → Action → Scope → Environment → Approval → Verification → Expiration



Material changes to the matrix MUST use a serialized process:



REQUEST → RESERVE → VALIDATE → COMMIT → VERIFY → CONFIRM



Concurrent changes affecting the same protected scope MUST NOT independently become authoritative.



2.4 Identifier Registry



The registry is the single source of truth for:



project IDs;



PBIM section IDs;



artifact IDs;



revisions;



supersession;



status;



owner;



canonical location.



Identifier collisions, unexplained reuse, or divergent registries MUST cause a governance stop until resolved.



2.5 Decision Ledger and ADRs



A material architectural or governance decision MUST have:



a decision identity;



an authoritative decision record;



supporting evidence;



applicable approval;



status;



supersession information.



Where ADRs are used, the Decision Ledger and ADR MUST reference each other.



No implementation may proceed from an unapproved material decision.



2.6 Protected Governance Resources



The following are protected:



PBIM baseline;



CA record;



Authority Register;



Authority–Permission Matrix;



identifier registry;



AEA/AEV/AEC/AECC records;



Decision Ledger;



authoritative ADRs;



requirements baseline;



Task Packet state;



evidence-integrity records;



gate records;



charter approval record.



Protected resources MUST NOT be silently overwritten.



3\. GOVERNANCE PROFILES AND MATERIALITY



3.1 Risk-Scaled Governance



PBIM uses:



LIGHT



For low-risk, reversible, non-sensitive work with limited blast radius.



STANDARD



For ordinary projects and changes requiring formal governance and assurance.



HIGH-ASSURANCE



For projects or changes involving significant:



financial impact;



payment systems;



authentication/authorization;



personal or sensitive data;



critical infrastructure;



safety;



regulated services;



high availability requirements;



irreversible migrations;



significant legal/compliance exposure.



The project MUST document why its profile applies.



3.2 Materiality Levels



A generic four-level model is used:



L0 — routine/non-material;



L1 — controlled project-level change;



L2 — material architectural, security, financial, data, compliance, or operational change;



L3 — critical/high-consequence change requiring the highest available governance and assurance.



An implementer MUST NOT unilaterally downgrade a material requirement or change.



3.3 Cumulative Materiality



Related low-risk changes MUST be assessed cumulatively.



A sequence of individually small changes MUST be escalated when their combined effect crosses a governance threshold.



Materiality MUST consider:



blast radius;



reversibility;



security;



privacy/data;



financial impact;



operational impact;



dependency impact;



legal/regulatory impact;



safety;



reputational impact.



3.4 Risk Record



Material risk classification MUST record:



risk profile;



rationale;



affected scope;



blast radius;



reversibility;



security impact;



data impact;



financial impact;



operational impact;



dependency impact;



legal/regulatory impact;



reviewer;



approval;



treatment;



residual risk.



4\. PBIM ARCHITECTURAL ENGINEERING ASSURANCE



4.1 Four-Artifact Assurance Cycle



For material PBIM architecture:



AEA — Architectural Engineering Analysis



AEV — Architectural Engineering Verification



AEC — Architectural Engineering Challenge



AECC — Architectural Engineering Challenge Closure



The four artifacts have different purposes.



AEA analyzes.



AEV verifies the proposed baseline.



AEC attacks the baseline.



AECC determines whether material findings have actually been resolved and records closure.



4.2 Independence



Independence MUST be evaluated rather than assumed.



The minimum independence dimensions are:



I1 organizational independence;



I2 evidence independence;



I3 technical independence;



I4 governance independence.



A person or agent with the same underlying authority, credentials, decision rights, or technical control cannot become independent merely by changing role labels.



If required independence is not achieved:



CHALLENGE-INDEPENDENCE-FAILED



The gate MUST stop or escalate according to the governance profile.



4.3 Evidence Independence



A challenger MUST have access to sufficient source evidence to test the claim.



Evidence that has been selectively summarized, rewritten, or withheld MUST NOT be treated as equivalent to independently reviewable source evidence.



4.4 AEV Decision States



The allowed AEV states are:



AEV APPROVE



AEV APPROVE WITH CONDITIONS



AEV RETURN



AEV BLOCK



ARCHITECTURAL RESET



The decision MUST include evidence, unresolved findings, conditions, and authorization boundaries.



4.5 AEC Closure



An AEC finding is not closed merely because wording changed.



Closure requires:



finding identity;



original severity;



root cause;



corrective action;



evidence of correction;



independent confirmation where required;



residual risk;



disposition;



approving authority.



5\. PROJECT BASE INTEGRATION INITIALIZATION



The following sections are the authoritative PBIM pre-charter sequence.





16\. PBIM CONTROL STATES



The following state progression is authoritative:



IDEA

→ PROJECT-REGISTERED

→ PBIM-BOOTSTRAPPED

→ PBIM-BASELINED

→ PROPOSAL-DRAFTED

→ PROPOSAL-BASELINED

→ PROJECT-TEMPLATE-DRAFTED

→ PROJECT-TEMPLATE-BASELINED

→ PROJECT-INITIALIZED

→ SIMULATION-READY

→ PBIM-ACTIVE-PRECHARTER

→ CHARTER-DRAFTED

→ CHARTER-APPROVED

→ PROJECT-LIFECYCLE-OWNS-GOVERNANCE



A project MUST NOT skip a mandatory gate without an explicitly authorized transition mechanism.



17\. DOCUMENT PRECEDENCE AND CONFLICT RESOLUTION



When project documents conflict, use this order:



applicable law/regulation/competent-authority requirement;



constitutional authority and organizational constitutional instruments;



approved Project Charter;



approved project governance framework/template;



approved PBIM baseline for pre-charter matters;



approved ADR/Decision Ledger records;



requirements and constraints baseline;



Task Packets;



implementation documentation;



agent instructions and derived summaries.



A lower-level artifact MUST NOT override a higher-level authority.



Where two artifacts at the same authority level conflict, the project MUST stop the affected decision until the conflict is resolved through the defined decision process.



18\. LOCAL JURISDICTION AND REGULATORY ADAPTATION



18.1 Jurisdiction-First Rule



PBIM MUST first identify the law, regulation, regulator, contractual obligation, licensing requirement, employment requirement, tax requirement, data/privacy requirement, cybersecurity requirement, sector rule, and procurement rule applicable in \[PROJECT-LOCATION].



Only after local requirements are identified should global standards be applied.



Global standards are reference frameworks unless legally, contractually, or organizationally adopted.



18.2 Ghana Baseline Example



When \[PROJECT-LOCATION] is in Ghana, the project should evaluate, as applicable:



Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843);



Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038);



Electronic Transactions Act, 2008 (Act 772), including applicable amendments;



Electronic Communications Act, 2008 (Act 775);



Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651);



sector-specific financial, payment, health, education, public-sector, or other regulations;



applicable Cyber Security Authority requirements;



applicable Data Protection Commission requirements;



applicable Bank of Ghana or other sector regulator requirements where relevant.



The list is illustrative, not automatically applicable to every project.



18.3 Legal Currency Rule



A legal or regulatory citation MUST be checked for current status before being used as a binding project requirement.



The project MUST record:



source;



effective date;



current status;



applicability;



responsible compliance owner;



evidence of assessment.



19\. MODERN PROJECT-MANAGEMENT ALIGNMENT



PBIM is aligned conceptually with modern project-management standards while remaining methodology-neutral.



The generic framework should be interpreted alongside:



PMI PMBOK Guide — Eighth Edition (2025) and the current Standard for Project Management;



ISO 21500:2021;



ISO 21502:2020 and its current revision status;



ISO 21505:2017 for governance;



ISO 21511:2018 for work-breakdown structures;



ISO 21512:2024 for earned-value implementation where applicable;



ISO 21506:2024 vocabulary;



ISO 31000:2018 for risk management;



applicable sector standards.



PBIM does not claim certification or compliance merely by citing these standards.



20\. SOFTWARE/ENGINEERING ASSURANCE BASELINE



Where the project includes software or digital systems, the project template SHOULD address:



secure requirements;



threat modeling;



architecture decision records;



source-control integrity;



code review;



dependency management;



secrets management;



least privilege;



automated tests;



integration tests;



security testing;



privacy controls;



observability;



backup/recovery;



deployment controls;



rollback;



change management;



release authorization;



operational readiness.



For high-assurance systems, evidence MUST be sufficient to demonstrate that the required control actually operated.



21\. OPERATIONAL READINESS PRINCIPLE



For systems that will eventually be released or operated, use:



IMPLEMENTATION-VERIFIED

→ OPERATIONALLY-READY

→ RELEASE-AUTHORIZED



Operational readiness SHOULD include evidence for:



monitoring;



alert ownership;



incident response;



backup;



tested recovery;



dependency availability;



rollback;



migration safety;



access control;



logging;



support ownership;



release authorization.



A backup that has never been restored is not sufficient evidence of recoverability.



A rollback procedure that cannot address data state is incomplete.



22\. RECOVERY AND FAILURE GOVERNANCE



PBIM MUST remain governed during failure.



Recovery scenarios include:



repository corruption;



evidence loss;



registry corruption;



credential compromise;



partial implementation;



failed migration;



failed rollback;



loss of an agent;



loss of a project authority;



loss/unavailability of CA;



compromised automation;



baseline drift.



Recovery MUST identify:



authority;



source of truth;



last valid baseline;



evidence;



restoration method;



validation;



independent verification;



reauthorization requirement.



Emergency action MUST NOT silently become permanent governance.



23\. AGENT OPERATING RULES



Agents MUST:



state their assigned role;



remain within authorized scope;



distinguish evidence from inference;



identify uncertainty;



preserve dissent;



avoid claiming authority they do not possess;



avoid claiming independence without evidence;



retain material source evidence;



respect protected baselines;



stop when a mandatory gate fails;



identify conflicts rather than silently resolving them;



produce reproducible outputs where feasible.



Agents MUST NOT:



self-approve their own material work where independent verification is required;



redefine governance authority;



bypass protected controls;



alter approved baselines without controlled change;



treat consensus as proof;



conceal negative findings;



downgrade risk merely to pass a gate;



continue after a mandatory stop without authorized resumption.



24\. STANDARD PROMPT STRUCTURE



Every PBIM prompt MUST contain:



A. Designated Target



Who is expected to act.



B. Objective



What the response must accomplish.



C. Authority Boundary



What the target may and may not decide.



D. Required Inputs



All documents/data that must be reviewed.



E. Analysis Requirements



The exact domains to inspect.



F. Required Output



The expected artifact and structure.



G. Evidence Requirements



What evidence must support claims.



H. Decision Vocabulary



Allowed gate states.



I. Failure Conditions



What blocks progression.



J. Publication/Storage



Where the output belongs.



K. Revision/Supersession



How the output is versioned and superseded.



L. Next Gate



The condition required to continue.



This standard replaces vague prompts that merely ask an agent to “review” a document.



25\. PBIM MAINTENANCE POLICY



PBIM maintenance is triggered by:



material changes in applicable law;



material changes in project-management standards;



major engineering/security practice changes;



major lessons learned;



AEC blockers;



repeated governance failures;



changes to organizational constitutional authority;



significant changes in AI-agent capabilities or permissions;



new project classes requiring different assurance.



Maintenance MUST NOT silently alter the active baseline.



The workflow is:



CHANGE PROPOSAL

→ AEA

→ AEV

→ AEC

→ AECC

→ NEW BASELINE

→ SUPERSESSION

Transition Rule



No active project should be forced to rewrite historical records merely to adopt v2.00.



Instead:

identify gaps;



remediate material gaps;



designate v2.00 as the new baseline where approved.

\[PROJECT-LOCATION] established.

28\. FINAL PBIM INTEGRATION STATEMENT



PBIM is complete when the project possesses a valid, approved Project Charter and the project is ready to operate under its selected project-management and engineering lifecycle.



The authoritative boundary is:



\[\[BASE-ID]-\[PROJECT-ID]]\[GOV-01-0004.1] — DEVELOP PROJECT CHARTER

Project Charter;



Project Management Plan / project operating model;



delivery lifecycle;



engineering lifecycle;



governance framework;



quality framework;



security/privacy framework;



procurement framework;



monitoring and control mechanisms.

execute the Project Proposal and Project Template stages;



develop and approve the Project Charter.



End of PBIM v2.00.00 Generic Baseline Candidate.







1.2 Governing Principles



Human accountability: AI agents may analyze, draft, verify and implement within authorized scope; accountable human authority remains responsible for consequential project decisions.



Authority is not capability: repository access, administrator privileges, or tool capability do not create governance authority.



Evidence before assertion: a document shall not claim that a control is enforced unless implementation evidence demonstrates enforcement.



Risk-scaled assurance: ceremony scales with project risk; protected controls do not disappear merely because a project is small.



Traceability: material decisions shall be traceable from source requirement or decision through artifact, review, implementation evidence and disposition.



Separation of duties: authorship, verification and adversarial challenge should be separated where practical; where independence is impossible, the limitation must be disclosed and compensated for.



No silent self-amendment: PBIM constitutional controls cannot be changed by an executor merely because the executor has technical access.



Stop is a valid state: uncertainty, scope escape, evidence failure, security exposure, or governance conflict can place work in STOPPED or BLOCKED state.



Durable evidence: authoritative references require durable identity, revision and integrity information.



Local-first compliance: applicable Ghanaian law and regulatory requirements are considered before global frameworks; global standards supplement rather than silently override local law.



Minimum necessary complexity: controls should solve a demonstrated risk without creating needless administrative machinery.



Reversibility: decisions and technical changes should preserve a feasible rollback or recovery path; irreversible operations require explicit authorization and recovery planning.



1.3 Control Maturity



PBIM uses four control states:



DESIGNED — specified in an approved document or template.



ENFORCEABLE — the specification is sufficiently precise to be mechanized or independently checked.



ENFORCED — operational controls demonstrably prevent or detect prohibited actions.



INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED — enforcement evidence has been independently examined and accepted.



A document must never represent DESIGNED or ENFORCEABLE controls as already ENFORCED.



1.4 Authority Model



The generic authority model is:



CA — external constitutional authority, only where the organization/project requires an authority above the project authority for protected governance rules.



H0 — accountable human project authority.



H1 — designated human reviewers/approvers.



H2 — AI/technical executors and collaborating agents.



SYSTEM — automated enforcement mechanisms such as CI, repository rules, task-scope checks and evidence validation.



CA is not mandatory for every project. If it is omitted, the Project Charter must identify the highest accountable authority and how constitutional/project governance changes are authorized.



If CA is used, its scope, appointment, term, independence and emergency/unavailability procedure must be explicitly recorded. Constitutional changes are blocked when the required authority is unavailable unless a separately approved external governance rule provides a safe escalation route.



1.5 Independence Record



For every formal AEV/AEC decision, record:



identity/role of reviewer;



whether the reviewer authored the target artifact;



repository and evidence permissions;



shared credentials or ownership, if any;



material conflicts of interest;



evidence source independence;



organizational independence status;



epistemic independence status;



any limitation on the reviewer's eligibility.



A role title alone does not establish independence.



1.6 Risk Profiles



LIGHT



For low-risk internal work with no material personal-data, financial, safety, security, or public-service consequences.



STANDARD



Default for ordinary business, software, integration and service projects.



HIGH-ASSURANCE



Required or strongly indicated where failure may materially affect safety, critical infrastructure, regulated personal data, significant financial transactions, security, public services, or legally protected interests.



The project may increase its profile at any time. It may not downgrade a profile merely to avoid a control.



2\. PBIM Evidence and Document-Control Rules



2.1 Source Classification



Every referenced artifact shall be classified as one of:



AUTHORITATIVE — approved source of truth;



CONTROLLED — draft under formal review;



REFERENCE — useful background material;



EVIDENCE — factual proof of an event/control;



DERIVED — generated from other controlled artifacts;



OBSOLETE — retained for history but not current authority.



2.2 Durable Reference Requirement



Authoritative references must identify:



repository/project;



path or durable document identifier;



revision/tag/branch where applicable;



immutable commit/object identifier or SHA-256 content hash where technically applicable;



publication timestamp;



status;



owner.



A branch name alone is insufficient for a critical approval reference.



2.3 Evidence Integrity



For high-assurance or materially contested decisions, retain raw evidence separately from sanitized summaries. Summaries may be used for readability but must never replace the underlying evidence required to reproduce the decision.



2.4 Single Authoritative State



A project must have one authoritative current state for each controlled artifact. Concurrent revisions must be serialized or explicitly reconciled before an artifact is treated as authoritative.



2.5 Decision Ledger



Material decisions should be recorded in a durable Decision Ledger with:



Decision-ID | Date | Authority | Question | Options | Decision | Rationale | Evidence | Conditions | Review/Expiry | Supersedes



3\. Local Regulatory and Standards Baseline



3.1 Ghana-First Rule



For projects located in Ghana, the legal/regulatory assessment begins with applicable Ghanaian law and competent regulators. International standards are used as engineering and governance references unless a Ghanaian law, regulation, license, directive or contractual obligation requires a different treatment.



The baseline shall be revalidated at project initiation and again at charter where the project remains subject to regulatory uncertainty.



3.2 Data Protection



Where personal data is processed, assess applicability of Ghana's data-protection regime, registration/notification requirements, controller/processor responsibilities, lawful processing, data-subject rights, retention, security and cross-border processing requirements.



The Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) remains an important legal reference; Ghana's later proposed data-protection legislation must be checked for enactment and commencement before relying on it as law. The PBIM must never assume that a bill is law merely because a draft exists.



3.3 Cybersecurity



Where cybersecurity activities or systems are involved, assess Ghana's Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), applicable Cyber Security Authority requirements, incident obligations, critical-information-infrastructure implications, cybersecurity service/provider obligations, and sector-specific requirements.



3.4 Electronic Transactions and Communications



Where electronic transactions, records, authentication, communications, payments or digital services are involved, assess applicable Ghanaian electronic-transactions and electronic-communications requirements and relevant regulator requirements.



3.5 Employment and Working Time



Where project staffing is governed by Ghanaian employment law, project-duration and work-planning assumptions must be checked against the applicable employment contract, Labour Act requirements, approved working arrangements, rest/leave requirements and any applicable collective or sector rules. PBIM shall not hard-code a universal daily/weekly work-hour number as a substitute for legal review.



3.6 Global Engineering Baseline



Depending on project risk and scope, consider current editions or applicable guidance from:



PMI PMBOK and applicable PMI standards;



ISO 9001 quality management;



ISO/IEC 27001 information-security management;



ISO/IEC 27002 security controls;



ISO 31000 risk management;



ISO/IEC 25010 software/product quality where relevant;



ISO/IEC 42001 AI management where AI governance is material;



OWASP guidance for web/application security;



applicable W3C accessibility and web standards;



applicable accounting, tax, procurement, health/safety, environmental and sector standards.



The applicable standard/version must be recorded rather than assumed.



3.7 Standards Transition Rule



If an existing project uses a legacy practice:



identify the legacy practice;



identify the current target practice;



explain the risk/gap;



define a transition control;



define the cut-over date or trigger;



preserve historical compatibility where necessary;



prohibit the legacy practice from becoming a new dependency unless explicitly approved.

PBIM uses a compact pre-charter sequence. It does not attempt to reproduce the entire project-management process catalogue as its own lifecycle.

15\. Cross-Cutting Governance Controls



15.1 Stop Conditions



PBIM work must stop when any of the following occurs:



authority is ambiguous for a consequential decision;



evidence is materially unreliable or unavailable;



scope escapes the authorized task;



secrets or sensitive data are exposed;



a material security/privacy issue is discovered;



a legal/regulatory obligation is uncertain in a way that could affect authorization;



a reviewer falsely claims independence;



two artifacts claim to be the authoritative state;



an irreversible action lacks approved recovery/authorization;



an AEC finding invalidates a load-bearing assumption.



15.2 Resume Conditions



A stopped task cannot resume merely because the executor decides to resume. The responsible authority must resolve the stop condition and record the decision.



15.3 Emergency Delegation



Emergency delegation must specify:



delegator;



delegate;



authority scope;



excluded powers;



start time;



expiry time;



evidence of appointment;



review authority;



automatic stop/expiry behavior.



A generic default maximum of 72 hours may be adopted for emergency delegation where appropriate, but the project must validate the period against its actual governance and legal requirements. Expired delegation automatically returns the affected governance state to STOPPED unless renewed by the competent authority.



15.4 Cumulative Materiality



Change classification must consider cumulative effect. A series of individually minor changes must be escalated when their combined effect crosses the project's materiality threshold.



15.5 Concurrency



Authoritative governance artifacts such as the authority-permission matrix, registry and Decision Ledger require a defined concurrency/serialization mechanism. Version control alone does not guarantee that the currently selected revision is the authoritative revision.



15.6 Root-of-Trust Limitation



Where an external constitutional authority is used, PBIM must explicitly acknowledge that compromise of that root is outside PBIM's own constitutional control boundary. The project/organization must define the external assurance and appointment controls protecting that authority.



16\. PBIM Maintenance and Versioning



16.1 Maintenance Triggers



Review PBIM when:



a major project-management standard changes;



applicable Ghanaian law/regulation changes;



the organization's governance model changes;



a material PBIM defect is discovered;



an AEC exposes a reusable architectural weakness;



project lessons reveal systemic failure;



the agent/tool ecosystem materially changes;



security/privacy practice changes materially.



16.2 Versioning



Use semantic-style document versions:



major — architectural/governance incompatibility or major lifecycle change;



minor — new capability/control without breaking the model;



patch — editorial, clarification or non-structural correction.



Every major/minor revision should retain its predecessor reference and decision rationale.



16.3 Change Register



CHANGE-ID | SECTION | OLD STATE | NEW STATE | REASON | EVIDENCE | AUTHORITY | EFFECTIVE DATE | TRANSITION | RISK



17\. Prompt Engineering Standard



Every PBIM prompt must contain, where applicable:



Target — Lead, Implementation, Reliability, Security, Human Authority, or multi-agent group.



Context — artifact being reviewed and current revision.



Objective — exact output required.



Inputs — authoritative source documents.



Constraints — legal, security, scope, privacy, architecture and project constraints.



Method — analysis/verification/challenge procedure.



Evidence rule — distinguish claims from evidence.



Decision vocabulary — fixed decision outcomes.



Output schema — required sections/fields.



Gate condition — what permits the workflow to continue.



Stop condition — what blocks or resets the workflow.



Independence disclosure — where verification/challenge is involved.



No-invention rule — missing facts become assumptions/questions, not fabricated values.



Durable reference rule — identify the exact artifact revision used.



Prompts should be optimized for deterministic, auditable responses rather than merely producing verbose analysis.



18\. Agent Collaboration Standard



The PBIM is multi-agent compatible but not multi-agent dependent.



18.1 Lead Agent



Responsible for orchestration, synthesis, architecture, conflict resolution and preparation of controlled baselines within authorized scope.



18.2 Implementation Agent



Responsible for implementation only after the project authorizes implementation through its post-charter governance and task controls.



18.3 Reliability/Verification Agent



Responsible for independent verification, test evidence, CI/reproducibility and operational-readiness evidence where assigned.



18.4 Security/Challenge Agent



Responsible for adversarial analysis, security review and challenge execution within authorized scope.



18.5 Human Authority



Retains accountability for project authorization, material scope, major financial commitments, security exceptions, production authorization, destructive actions, regulatory decisions and project closure.



19\. PBIM Decision States



State



Meaning



DRAFT

CONTROLLED

AEV-APPROVED

AEC-PASS-WITH-AMENDMENTS

APPROVED

CHARTER-READY

HANDED-OFF

20\. PBIM Closure Checklist



Before 0004.1, confirm:



Project identity established.



Project location established.



Local legal/regulatory assessment performed.



Risk profile assigned.



Authority structure established.



PBIM baseline verified/challenged.



Project Proposal established and accepted.



Project Proposal assurance completed.



Project Template generated and accepted.



Project Template assurance completed.



Project environment configured.



Agent/task controls configured where required.



Evidence/document-control system configured.



Simulation completed.



Material simulation findings resolved or explicitly accepted.



Charter package prepared.



Human project authority identified.



Charter meeting/decision process established.



PBIM handoff record prepared.



21\. Reference Standards and Legal Baseline



The generic PBIM should be maintained against current applicable sources, including:



Ghana Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), and any subsequently enacted replacement/amendment in force at the project date.



Ghana Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), and applicable Cyber Security Authority requirements.



Ghana Electronic Transactions Act, 2008 (Act 772), where applicable.



Ghana Electronic Communications Act, 2008 (Act 775), where applicable.



Applicable Ghana labour/employment requirements.



Applicable Ghana tax, procurement, health and safety, environmental and sector-specific requirements.



PMI PMBOK Guide — Eighth Edition (2025) and applicable current PMI standards.



Applicable ISO/IEC, ISO, OWASP, W3C and other engineering standards selected according to project risk and scope.



Legal-status rule: a draft bill, proposed standard or discussion document shall not be treated as binding law. The project must verify enactment, commencement and applicability before treating it as a mandatory legal requirement.



22\. Reference-Set Integrity Note



This PBIM revision was developed from the supplied PBIM reference family consisting of:



current PBIM baseline;



PBIM AEA Query;



consolidated PBIM AEA reports;



PBIM AEV Statement revisions;



PBIM AEV responses;



PBIM AEC Adversarial Duel revisions;



PBIM AEC results.



The reference family demonstrates a mature architectural direction: explicit authority boundaries, control-maturity separation, durable evidence, independent verification, adversarial challenge, risk-scaled governance, stop/reset controls and human accountability. It also demonstrates why PBIM should not treat numeric challenge scores as sufficient by themselves. The fresh adversarial evidence identified material weaknesses involving durable references, task-scope enforcement, emergency delegation, independence detection, concurrency, cumulative materiality and root-of-trust limitations; these are therefore represented as explicit generic controls or implementation verification requirements in this revision.



23\. Final PBIM Boundary Statement



PBIM is complete when the project has a controlled, reviewed, challenged and charter-ready basis for authorization. PBIM is not the project itself.



The official integration boundary is:



\[\[BASE-ID]-\[PROJECT-ID]]\[GOV-01-0004.1] Initiate Project or Phase (Develop Project Charter)



Upon approval of the Project Charter, the PBIM transfers governance context, evidence, decisions, assumptions, risks, constraints and the tailored Project Template into the project. Subsequent project execution, planning, monitoring, control and closure are governed by the approved project framework rather than by additional PBIM identifiers.
